name: otter

attributes.attribute: white patch under the jaw was its only weakness
avenged the slayer of their king
a scrap of hide guarded the household

sources: MacGregor, Alasdair Alpin. The PeatFire Flame: Folk-Tales and Traditions of the Highlands & Islands. Edinburgh: The Moray Press, 1937, 132.
Ó hÓgain, Dáithí. Irish Superstitions. London: Gill & Macmillan, 1995, 55-57.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The otter sat in the lore of Ireland and the Highland Scots as a portent tied to the place of the dead. A king of that race, the Dorraghor or the Dobharch nigh, drew the colony through the water. That ruler's pelt sold for a sum past any coin. A white mark under the jaw was the one place a weapon could reach, for the rest of the skin stayed proof against harm. The hunter who slew that king paid the debt with his own life, so the kin declared. A sliver of the pelt kept near the door warded the whole household. At the rout of Culloden the story let the men carrying the hide walk away safe.

okr.objective: Tell of the king otter, whose pelt guarded a home and the soldier who carried it.
key_results: The otter was a portent bound into the night behind.
The king's pelt sold for a fortune.
A patch of hide kept the household from harm.
The death of the king cost the killer's own ending.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
